prompt: What does logical replication send to the receiving server?

choices.text: The write-ahead log, byte for byte
choices.why: That is physical replication.

choices.text: A fresh pg_dump of the database each minute
choices.why: Nothing is dumped after the first copy of the rows.

choices.text: Row changes for the published tables
choices.why: Right: inserts, updates and deletes, decoded from the write-ahead log.

choices.text: Copies of the changed data files
choices.why: Files are physical; logical replication sends rows.

prompt: Match each property with the kind of replication it describes.
hint: One of each pair belongs to each kind.

pairs.left: Copies the whole cluster as files
Lets the copy run another major version
Copies table definitions as they change
pairs.right: Physical, as part of the files

prompt: Why must a physical standby run the same major version as its primary?

choices.text: The log is in that version's format
choices.why: Right: it replays files and log written by that version, and a different version reads a different format.

choices.text: The replication protocol checks a licence
choices.why: There is no licence check.

choices.text: Slots exist only in the newest version
choices.why: Slots have existed since version 9.4.

choices.text: Because standbys cannot run queries otherwise
choices.why: Query support has nothing to do with the version match.

prompt: The server that offers tables is the publisher; the server that receives them through a subscription is the ___.
What did the publisher need before logical decoding could work?

choices.text: A replication slot created by hand
choices.why: The subscription created its slot by itself.

choices.text: archive_mode = on
choices.why: Logical replication streams; it does not need the archive.

choices.text: A second data directory
choices.why: The publisher is the same server.

choices.text: wal_level = logical
choices.why: Right: the default, replica, does not carry enough to rebuild rows.

prompt: Why was `replicator` given `SELECT` on the two tables?

choices.text: Logical replication runs as a superuser otherwise
choices.why: It runs as the role in the connection string.

choices.text: For the first copy of their rows
choices.why: Right: a subscription begins with a plain copy of each table, which needs read access.

choices.text: SELECT includes the REPLICATION right
choices.why: Those are separate rights.

choices.text: The publication cannot be created without it
choices.why: The publication was created before the grant.

prompt: What must exist on the subscriber before `CREATE SUBSCRIPTION`?

choices.text: The publisher's roles
choices.why: The schema was loaded without owners, so no roles were needed.

choices.text: The tables, with their columns
choices.why: Right: the schema is copied first; rows go into tables that already exist.

choices.text: A physical standby of the publisher
choices.why: The subscriber is an independent server.

choices.text: A slot on the subscriber
choices.why: The slot is created on the publisher.

prompt: Match each `pg_dump` option used for the schema copy to what it leaves out.
hint: Three things that belong to the publisher.

pairs.right: Owners naming roles 17 does not have

prompt: Why does the lesson run `chmod 600 ~/.pgpass`?

choices.text: Docker cannot read files with other permissions
choices.why: Docker never reads it; psql does.

choices.text: PostgreSQL 17 requires it
choices.why: It is the client that checks.

choices.text: To encrypt the passwords in it
choices.why: chmod changes permissions; the file stays plain text.

choices.text: psql ignores a file readable by others
choices.why: Right: it refuses to use a file with looser permissions.

prompt: The subscription created a slot on the publisher. What does that mean if the subscriber stops for a week?

choices.text: The publisher keeps every byte of log for it
choices.why: Right: like a physical slot, it holds the log until the subscriber consumes it, unless capped.

choices.text: The slot is dropped after an hour
choices.why: Slots are never dropped by themselves.

choices.text: The subscriber catches up from the archive
choices.why: A logical subscription reads from the slot, not from the archive.

choices.text: Nothing; logical slots hold no log
choices.why: They hold it exactly as physical slots do.

prompt: `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note` ran on the publisher, then an insert used it. What happened on the 17?

choices.text: The column was added automatically
choices.why: DDL is not replicated.

choices.text: The row arrived without its note
choices.why: The subscriber refused the row; nothing arrived.

choices.text: The apply failed: missing replicated column
choices.why: Right: the subscription stopped and retried, and nothing more arrived.

choices.text: The publisher refused the ALTER
choices.why: The publisher has no idea what its subscribers hold.

prompt: A release adds a column to a replicated table. Put the steps in the order that never stops the subscription.
hint: Who must be ready to receive it?
items: Add the column on the subscriber
Add the column on the publisher
Deploy the application that writes it
trap: Adding on the publisher first is what stopped the subscription in the lesson.

prompt: While the subscription was failing on the missing column, what was the slot on the publisher doing?

choices.text: Discarding the log it could not deliver
choices.why: A slot never discards what its consumer has not confirmed.

choices.text: Sending the rows to the archive instead
choices.why: Slots do not archive.

choices.text: Nothing; a failed subscription drops its slot
choices.why: The slot stays until somebody drops it.

choices.text: Holding all log from the failed change on
choices.why: Right: 336 bytes there, a full disk on a busy server.

prompt: The 17 has all 50,002 orders, yet its first insert failed with `Key (id)=(1) already exists`. Why?
hint: Is a sequence's value a row?

choices.text: The ids were replicated as text
choices.why: They are bigint on both servers.

choices.text: The primary key was not copied
choices.why: It was, by the schema dump, and it is what raised the error.

choices.text: Sequences are not replicated
choices.why: Right: rows arrived with their ids set, and the sequence itself never moved from 1.

choices.text: Version 17 restarts all sequences
choices.why: Nothing restarted; it was never advanced.

prompt: The shop has 1000 customers spread evenly over four cities. How many rows did the subscription to `recife_pub` receive?
Which feature limits a publication to the customers of one city?

choices.text: A row filter in the publication
choices.why: Right: a WHERE clause on the table, FOR TABLE customers WHERE (city = 'Recife').

choices.text: A view on the subscriber
choices.why: The subscriber would still receive every row.

choices.text: A separate database per city on the publisher
choices.why: Possible, and much more work than a filter.

choices.text: Row-level security
choices.why: That restricts queries, not what is published.

prompt: Where does a logical subscription appear for lesson 13's `lagcheck.sh`?
hint: It is a WAL sender on the publisher too.

choices.text: Nowhere; it needs a different check
choices.why: It appears in the same view.

choices.text: In pg_stat_replication, by its name
choices.why: Right: application_name is the subscription's name.

choices.text: Only in pg_stat_subscription on the subscriber
choices.why: That is the subscriber's view; the publisher has its own row.

choices.text: In pg_replication_slots only
choices.why: The slot is there, and so is a row in pg_stat_replication.

prompt: Put the upgrade's switch in order.
hint: Writes stop first; the application moves last.
items: Wait until the slot is 0 bytes behind
Move every sequence on the 17 past the 16's highest value
trap: Moving the sequences before writes stop leaves room for an id the 16 hands out afterwards.

prompt: The highest order id on the 16 was 50002 and the sequence was set to that plus 1000. What id did the first order on the 17 get?
hint: setval sets the last value used.

prompt: Why move the sequence to the highest id plus a thousand, rather than to the highest id?
hint: What can happen between reading the maximum and moving?

choices.text: Sequences only accept round numbers
choices.why: Any value works.

choices.text: PostgreSQL 17 reserves a thousand ids
choices.why: It reserves nothing.

choices.text: A cheap margin for an insert that sneaked in
choices.why: Right: gaps in ids cost nothing; a collision stops the application.

choices.text: To make the ids from the 17 recognisable
choices.why: That is a side effect, not the reason.

prompt: After the switch, what does the lesson say to do with the 16?

choices.text: Keep it, untouched, for now
choices.why: Right: until the 17 is trusted, it is the way back.

choices.text: Drop it at once to free the disk
choices.why: Then a problem with the 17 has no way back.

choices.text: Turn it into a standby of the 17
choices.why: A physical standby must run the same version.

choices.text: Subscribe it to the 17 at once
choices.why: Possible as a later step, not what the lesson says.

prompt: Which job needs logical replication rather than a physical standby?
hint: Version, part of the data, or writable.

choices.text: Failing over within seconds if the primary dies
choices.why: That is exactly what a physical standby is for.

choices.text: Keeping a byte-for-byte copy of every database
choices.why: That is physical.

choices.text: Reading reports from a read-only copy
choices.why: A physical standby serves reads.

choices.text: Moving the shop from version 16 to 17 in minutes
choices.why: Right: only logical replication crosses major versions.
